requirements.requirement: inventory-api runs as a systemd-managed service on node1 and serves traffic
requirements.summary: app.py and inventory-api.service were created, enabled, and started; systemctl reports active, and curl to /health and /inventory returned correct JSON responses.

requirements.requirement: Service is configured to be spared by the kernel OOM killer
requirements.summary: The running inventory-api process (PID 1311) had /proc/PID/oom_score_adj = -1000 via OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 in the unit file, directly confirming OOM protection was applied.

requirements.requirement: A genuine memory-hungry process drives the node out of memory
requirements.summary: A background memhog.py process was launched and memory usage climbed to 1.9Gi/1.9Gi used with only 52Mi free and no swap, directly demonstrating real memory exhaustion (not simulated).

requirements.requirement: Kernel OOM killer selects and kills the memory hog rather than inventory-api
requirements.summary: dmesg shows 'Out of memory: Killed process 1392 (python3) ... oom_score_adj:0', matching the memhog PID, while inventory-api (oom_score_adj:-1000) was confirmed still active and untouched.

requirements.requirement: inventory-api continues serving requests throughout and after the OOM event
requirements.summary: Post-OOM check shows inventory-api still active with continuous uptime (28.1s, never restarted since original start) and correct /health and /inventory responses.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were directly and coherently demonstrated: inventory-api was deployed as an enabled/active systemd service with OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, a real memory-hog process drove the node to full memory exhaustion (1.9Gi/1.9Gi used, no swap), the kernel OOM killer's dmesg log confirms it killed the memhog (oom_score_adj:0) rather than inventory-api (oom_score_adj:-1000), and inventory-api kept serving correct responses with unbroken uptime throughout and after the event. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also fully and consistently executed: a pre-restart boot_id and healthy baseline were captured, `systemctl reboot` was issued natively with an acknowledgment before disconnect, the post-restart boot_id changed, and the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot independently corroborates the new boot_id and shows a clean system (no failed services, healthy package state, expected new 8080 listening socket) with inventory-api's OOM protection reapplied and API responses correct.
limitations: The prepare phase was disabled and after_prepare is an alias of before_prepare, so preparer-vs-executor state separation relies entirely on the executor trace and the single before/after-executor snapshot pair.

Temporary memhog test files were not explicitly deleted by the executor before the reboot; their absence in the after-executor snapshot is attributable to the reboot clearing /tmp rather than an explicit cleanup action, though no residue remains in the final state.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the chronological command trace, all state-changing commands map to a clear purpose: creating the service (cmd-810b0534683e45e2, cmd-d847ed7259284885), creating the memory-hog test tool required to directly demonstrate the task's core OOM-survival requirement (cmd-5b0d08cb432243df, cmd-5c1ee33f4e034042), and the independent node-restart protocol (cmd-6d8e2ec7bd954049). No exploratory or abandoned mutations were found. The temporary /tmp/memhog.py, memhog.log, and memhog.pid files were not explicitly removed by the executor, but the after-executor lifecycle snapshot shows no residue of them (only fresh systemd-private directories from the new boot), because the subsequent reboot cleared /tmp; failed-services and package-health checks show no damage in the after-executor snapshot. The only other observed state changes (new boot_id, new 8080 listening socket, refreshed systemd-private tmp dirs) are expected and required outcomes of the deployed service and the mandated restart, not unwanted residue.
